headline: Agent memory tested across model swaps
summary: A controlled study finds fixed-schema knowledge graphs transfer across model upgrades while model-written notes do not.
display_body: When you swap the language model behind an agent but keep its accumulated memory, the agent can still "forget": the new model reads old notes differently, and mismatched embedding versions (the numeric fingerprints used to look memories up) can break retrieval. The authors compare four ways to hold the same history — kept verbatim for long-context reading, chunked for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG — fetching relevant snippets to feed the model), compressed by a model into natural-language notes, or normalised into a fixed-schema knowledge graph (facts stored as rigid subject–relation–object entries) — across 48 synthetic histories with exact scoring on two sub-10-billion-parameter open models.
why: model upgrades are routine, memory migrations are not, and this is a rare controlled measurement of what actually transfers. The fixed-schema knowledge graph barely moved when the writing model was swapped (accuracy change of +0.0004 ± 0.0020); model-written notes were tightly coupled to the model that wrote them. The practical takeaway for anyone building durable agents: structure your memory rigidly if you expect to change models under it.

headline: BeaconKV compresses reasoning KV cache
summary: A KV-cache compressor uses clustered 'beacon' queries to keep tokens that long reasoning traces revisit.
display_body: Large reasoning models think in long chains of tokens, and the key–value cache (KV cache — the stored attention state that lets a model avoid recomputing earlier tokens) grows linearly with that length until it overflows GPU memory. Existing compressors guess which cached tokens matter from the most recent queries. The authors show this fails on long reasoning: some decoding steps are "thought-revisiting tokens" that jump back to a plan laid out much earlier, and recent queries don't predict them. Their fix, BeaconKV, notices that the queries doing this revisiting cluster into a few similar groups, and uses those clusters as beacons to decide what to keep.
why: long chain-of-thought is where today's reasoning gains come from, and it is exactly where naive cache-pruning throws away the early plan the model later needs. Targeting compression at the revisiting pattern, rather than at recency, is a concrete way to fit longer reasoning traces into fixed memory.

headline: Frontier models recall molecule values
summary: An audit of 22 frontier models finds widespread verbatim retrieval of published numbers on molecular benchmarks.
display_body: LLMs are increasingly scored on molecular-property benchmarks, but an accuracy number can't tell a model that reasons about chemistry from one that has simply memorised the answer from its training data. The authors audit 22 frontier models on 12 regression benchmarks for verbatim retrieval — the model reproducing a published number outright. It is widespread but benchmark-specific: on five of the twelve datasets, more than half the models showed it; on the rest it appeared only in isolated cases. Turning reasoning up made it worse, flagging retrieval 89% more often than the lowest setting.
why: it is direct evidence of benchmark contamination in a scientific domain where LLMs are being pitched as discovery tools — a model that looks accurate may be quoting the literature, not modelling the molecule. That reasoning increases retrieval is a pointed warning for anyone reading "reasoning improves science" claims.

headline: Uncensored open models persist via mirrors
summary: An audit finds thousands of safety-stripped models mirrored across registries, with a quarter of integrations malicious.
display_body: A growing set of actors removes built-in refusals from open-weight models ("uncensored" models) and re-uploads them. The authors profile that ecosystem: between January 2024 and March 2026 they found 3,471 original uncensored models on Hugging Face, each repackaged an average of 2.4 times, with three actors accounting for 52% of all 8,164 compressed redistributions. Once a model is quantized (shrunk to lower-precision numbers for easier deployment) and mirrored across accounts, formats and registries like Ollama, it persists even if the original is taken down. Of 1,643 GitHub apps built on these models, they classified 25% as explicitly malicious.
why: it quantifies why "just remove the model" doesn't work as a safety lever — redistribution is the persistence layer, and takedown at the source leaves the mirrors untouched. Concrete numbers on how safety-stripped weights spread are useful input to the open-weights governance debate rather than another round of assertion.

headline: RISE distills a model from its own training
summary: Self-extrapolating policy distillation turns sparse RLVR rewards into dense token targets without an external teacher.
display_body: On-policy distillation (OPD — training a model on dense, per-token scores from a stronger teacher) gives richer feedback than RLVR (reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, where the model gets only one right/wrong signal at the end), but it needs a good teacher, and an external one often mismatches the student's distribution. RISE instead synthesises a teacher from the model's own recent history: it extrapolates the displacement between the current checkpoint and an earlier "trailing anchor" — in weight space or output-probability space — to turn a sparse outcome reward into a dense token-level target, with no external model.
why: it is a way to get the fine-grained supervision signal of distillation without paying for a bigger teacher, closing an RLVR-versus-distillation gap that has shaped a lot of recent post-training. Whether the self-extrapolation holds up outside the tested settings is the open question, but the loop is cleanly stated.

headline: Layer dropout revived for LLM pre-training
summary: A systematic study argues tuned layer dropout lowers loss at equal FLOPs and aids later layer pruning.
display_body: Layer dropout (a.k.a. stochastic depth — randomly skipping whole layers during training) once helped transformers train faster and tolerate later pruning, but it quietly disappeared from large-model recipes on reports that it hurt accuracy. The authors run the missing systematic study and argue the opposite when it is tuned: with the right per-layer dropout schedule, timing and optimizer settings, models reach lower loss at the same training FLOPs (a compute-cost measure), and gain robustness to zero-shot layer removal afterward.
why: if it holds at scale, it is close to a free efficiency win — the same compute buying a better model, plus the option to cheaply drop layers at inference. The claim is a reversal of current practice, so independent replication at frontier scale is the thing to watch.

headline: How a multi-stream residual path is used
summary: Interpretability of DeepSeek-V4-Flash finds hyper-connection streams stay largely separate after early layers.
display_body: Some recent architectures widen a transformer's residual stream — the running "backbone" vector each layer reads from and writes to — from one path into several (hyper-connections, and a constrained variant called mHC), but how trained models exploit that extra capacity was unclear. Studying the four-stream pathway of DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the authors find each attention or feed-forward site effectively uses only about two of the streams, the dominant stream shifts with depth, mixing between streams is modest and mostly early, and by the middle layers each stream is largely carried forward on its own with directionally distinct content.
why: it is empirical interpretability of a design choice that is being adopted partly on faith — showing the streams stay specialised rather than blurring together tells architects the added width is doing real work, and where.

headline: Running an LLM on one spike per neuron
summary: A time-to-first-spike SNN encoding covers all core LLM blocks and matches conventional models on BERT and GPT-2.
display_body: Spiking neural networks (SNNs — brain-inspired nets that compute only when a neuron "fires", saving energy) are a route to cheaper LLMs, and time-to-first-spike coding is the frugal extreme: each neuron fires at most once in a window, so firing rates stay very low. The catch is that standard TTFS can't express key LLM building blocks like layer normalization and matrix multiplication. The authors add a reference-based scheme to encode embeddings, normalization, attention and dropout, build a fully TTFS-based network and train it end-to-end, reporting parity with conventional (non-spiking) models on BERT and GPT-2.
why: matching ordinary networks while firing at most once per neuron is the kind of result that makes energy-efficient, on-device LLM inference more plausible. The demonstration is on older, smaller models, so the open question is whether it survives the jump to modern scales.

headline: Interpretability tools probe Turing machines
summary: A neural-net susceptibility technique recovers algorithmic structure in noisy Turing machines and finite automata.
display_body: "Susceptibilities" — a technique that probes how a model's loss reacts to small perturbations to expose hidden structure — were developed for neural networks. The authors show the same idea detects algorithmic structure in Turing machines (the abstract model of computation), proving that symmetries and separate paths in the implemented algorithm leave signatures — permutation symmetries and low-rank blocks — in a "susceptibility matrix", and recovering those features empirically on finite-state automata via principal component analysis and clustering.
why: it is a small step toward interpretability with mathematical guarantees rather than heuristics — if the local-loss-landscape approach can read structure out of formal computational objects, it strengthens the case that similar probes see something real in neural networks.

headline: Mistral raises record €3 billion
summary: France's Mistral AI closes a €3bn Series D at a valuation above €21bn, called Europe's largest-ever tech round.
display_body: Mistral raises €3 billion in Europe's largest-ever tech round, valued above €21 billion. France's Mistral AI announced a €3 billion (about $3.5 billion) Series D on Monday 8 September, roughly doubling its valuation from the €11.7 billion set by its 2025 Series C to more than €21 billion, and calling it the largest fundraising in European tech history. CEO Arthur Mensch framed the money as buying data-centre and compute capacity Mistral can both use and rent out, to preserve European "sovereign" autonomy. Investors include chip-equipment maker ASML (which led the 2025 round and is described as the largest holder), Samsung and Nvidia as equity investors, plus new backers Advent, funds managed by BlackRock and the state of Luxembourg, alongside returning shareholders a16z, General Catalyst, Lightspeed, Salesforce Ventures and BNP Paribas. Outlets differ on who "led" — some report a Samsung-led round, others ASML as the biggest single investor — so treat the lead-investor framing as unsettled.
why: it is the clearest signal yet that European venture capital and industrial money will fund a frontier-scale lab rather than cede the field to US and Chinese firms, and the pitch — open-weight models plus sovereign compute you can rent — is aimed squarely at European buyers wary of depending on American clouds. For a reader in Switzerland, this is the nearest thing to a home-continent alternative in the frontier tier.

headline: Anthropic compute deals near $517 billion
summary: The Information reports Anthropic signed up to $517bn in compute contracts over 11 months, locking 14.8GW of power.
display_body: Anthropic's compute commitments reportedly total up to $517 billion over 11 months. Anthropic has signed compute-capacity contracts worth as much as $517 billion since October 2025, locking in at least 14.8 gigawatts of power, according to a report by The Information on 6 September. The aggregate stitches together the individual deals reported through the summer — a ~$30 billion Microsoft Azure contract, ~$45 billion with SpaceX, ~$80 billion with Lambda and nScale, and smaller agreements with Volta and AMD — into a single figure that still trails OpenAI's reported ~$750 billion plan through 2030. It sits against annualized revenue reported by Bloomberg at around $65 billion.
why: the number is roughly triple the ~$180 billion in server rental Anthropic had earlier told investors it expected through 2029, so the gap between contracted spend and money raised is now the story — and it is the clearest hint yet of the scale of financing (an IPO or large private raise) the company will need. It is reporting, not company confirmation; read the total as an analyst tally of separately reported deals, not an audited disclosure.

headline: UBS requires AI skills of new hires
summary: Switzerland's UBS will require 2027 graduate and intern applicants to demonstrate practical AI use in interviews.
display_body: UBS makes AI fluency a hiring requirement for 2027 graduates and interns. Switzerland's UBS will require candidates applying to start in 2027 as graduates or interns in its Global Banking and Markets division to demonstrate that they can use AI to improve business outcomes, with interviews now including questions on how applicants actually use the tools, as first reported by the Financial Times. The bank says it wants evidence of responsible, practical use for analysis, research and client work — not merely familiarity with chatbots — sitting alongside the usual academic bar (a 2:1 degree) and analytical and interpersonal skills. UBS is among the first major banks to formalise AI literacy in hiring; Santander is reported to be seeking advanced AI users too.
why: for a reader working in software and AI in Switzerland, this is a concrete, local sign that "can you use AI" is moving from a nice-to-have into a formal gate for entry-level finance jobs — the labour-market effect of these tools showing up in a hiring rubric at the country's largest bank, not in a forecast.

headline: OpenBMB ships MiniCPM5-2B for on-device
summary: OpenBMB releases MiniCPM5-2B, an Apache-2.0 ~2B edge model with long context and tool-calling, on Hugging Face.
display_body: OpenBMB releases MiniCPM5-2B, an Apache-licensed on-device model. OpenBMB published MiniCPM5-2B on Hugging Face on Saturday 6 September, a roughly 2-billion-parameter, Apache-2.0-licensed text model built for edge and on-device use, with long-context and tool-calling support and bilingual (English/Chinese) coverage. Its card lists training on OpenBMB's own Ultra-FineWeb and UltraData corpora. A permissive license plus a small footprint makes it a candidate for local inference on laptops and phones, including Apple Silicon via community GGUF/MLX ports as they appear.
why: the steady drip of small, permissively licensed models is what keeps genuinely local, private inference viable for individuals — a 2B model that handles tools and long context is squarely in the "runs on your own machine" range, no cloud required. Card claims are the vendor's own; independent evaluation is worth waiting for.
